**Device:** NVIDIA L4 (compute capability 8.9, 58 SMs). **Peak FP64:** 473 G FLOP/s. Medians of 3 to 9 rounds per arm, each arm in its own process (rounds stop at IQR/median <= 2 %); IQR in parentheses.

**Workload:** two-body Kepler orbits (mu = 1, float64) from periapsis, a = 1, e uniform in [0, 0.9] (uniform: e = 0.45), random orientation; adaptive RKF7(8) (Fehlberg's tableau, a mixed absolute/relative max-norm error control and a standard step-size controller). Tolerance rtol = atol = 1e-10; final time 64 (10.2 periods). 1106 FLOP per attempt.

| arm | loop structure | lines of code |
|---|---|---:|
| hawk + eagle persistent | ONE launch, no graph, no map, no policy kernel: a grid sized from the SM count and the kernel's occupancy, each lane fetching base + atomicAdd(counter, 1) whenever its sample is done | 22 |
| eagle.simulate (eagle picks the launch mode) | eagle.simulate takes the kernel, its state and its parameters by name; eagle's automatic policy picks the launch mode from the batch (one launch for a small batch, the persistent launch above it); the row records the mode taken | 21 |
| eagle graph | one CUDA graph: device WHILE loop of the attempt kernel, which marks and counts its finished samples and runs the attempts per launch eagle's policy picks; finished samples skipped by the Terminated guard | 22 |
| Warp per-thread kernel | one launch: each thread loops over its own sample's attempts to the final time | 74 |
| JAX jit(vmap(while_loop)) | one compiled executable: per-sample while loop, batched (runs until the slowest sample finishes) | 25 |
| PyTorch torch.compile (reduce-overhead) | host loop: a block of 16 masked attempts compiled by Inductor (Triton) and replayed as a CUDA graph, host check per block | 46 |
| CuPy masked | host loop: one masked whole-batch attempt (array expressions), host check per attempt | 25 |
| PyTorch + CUDA graph | host loop: a CUDA graph of 16 masked attempts replayed, host check per block | 53 |

### Agreement with the analytic orbit

Every arm, every sample: final time reached exactly; position error against the analytic Kepler state (Newton on Kepler's equation to machine precision) below the stated bound n_acc tol (1 + v_p)(1 + 6 pi n_orbits v_p), derived from the controller's per-step budget and the Kepler along-track amplification (see truth_bound; not fitted). The truth check runs in the arm's own process; the step counts it returns are compared with the reference arm (eagle graph) in the parent: any difference comes from a floating-point difference flipping one accept/reject decision.

### Where each tool fits

Each tool here solves the same 13-stage adaptive problem to the same tolerance and agrees with the analytic orbit; they differ in how the per-sample control flow is written and run. Numbers below are at N = 1,000,000; the fastest arm there is eagle.simulate (eagle picks the launch mode) (2.32 s).

- **hawk + eagle persistent.** the plain (not active-set) attempt kernel, forced through hawk's persist entry: one launch, no graph, no map, no policy kernel -- a grid of SMs blocks of 256 lanes steals the next unfinished sample off a counter when their own finishes: 2.32 s; the eagle graph takes 1.69× as long.
- **eagle.simulate (eagle picks the launch mode).** the same kernel through eagle.simulate, its state and parameters by name (21 lines with the kernel): 2.32 s; the eagle graph takes 1.69× as long.
- **eagle graph.** the attempt is per-sample scalar code (22 lines with its launch; the kernel finishes its own samples), one kernel per attempt looped on the device: 3.91 s.
- **Warp per-thread kernel.** an explicit per-thread loop in a Python-embedded kernel language (74 lines, its own stages): 4.26 s.
- **JAX jit(vmap(while_loop)).** writes the per-sample loop directly (25 lines) and compiles the whole batch into one executable: 7.24 s.
- **PyTorch torch.compile (reduce-overhead).** compiles a block of 16 masked attempts with torch.compile (reduce-overhead): –; eager PyTorch takes – as long.
- **CuPy masked.** array code in the NumPy style (25 lines), the control flow as masks over the batch: 52.8 s.
- **PyTorch + CUDA graph.** records 16 attempts as a CUDA graph and replays them, removing per-kernel launch cost: 55.3 s; eager PyTorch takes – as long.

### Memory method

A separate pass after the timing pass. Each (arm, N) runs in a fresh process: imports, the CUDA context created by one tiny device operation, then the baseline read, before the arm builds or allocates anything; then the arm's kernels built and a warm-up run on a 64-sample batch (every compile happens here; JAX also compiles for shape N), so every library's pool reserved during the warm-up counts in the reading; CuPy's pools and PyTorch's cache trimmed after the warm-up; then the arm built for N (eagle's graph, PyTorch's captured graph) and one full run with upload and download, the device read every 2 ms throughout (the masked arms hand their temporaries back after each run, so a reading after it would miss them). Device: the most memory NVML accounted to the process on the timed GPU during the build and the run, minus the baseline. Caveats: each allocator's rounding and growth policy count (JAX's allocator grows in regions that can exceed the request; PyTorch rounds blocks up and a captured CUDA graph keeps a private pool; Warp's stream-ordered pool reserves in chunks of tens of MiB, its release threshold set to 0 after the warm-up); the driver accounts in pages of about 2 MiB, so small-N rows read 0 or one page. Host: the peak resident set (VmHWM, reset to the current RSS at the host baseline, taken after the warm-up) minus the baseline RSS. Minimum: the planes the workload needs, N x (8 float64 planes (state, time, step) x 8 bytes + 2 counters x 4 bytes) = N x 72 bytes.
